It is reminiscent of the kiki/bouba effect. You may notice this across languages as well. In Spanish, "suave" is soft, and "duro" is hard.

You could even extend this to more abstract concepts. Like a dream itself, the word "dream" uses softer sounds and barely sits on your lips before disappearing, just like a dream might escape you in the morning. "Reality" uses harder sounds, makes you do more work with your tongue to generate the "t" sound; this makes sense considering reality is about being more physically grounded - it is a concrete concept.

Of course it does not work for every word, but it works for many.

Other examples:

  • fluffy/scratchy
  • harmony/discord
  • silky/rough
  • symphony/cacophony
  • love/hate
Have you ever noticed how the sounds of some words accurately represent their meanings? "Soft" easily flows from the lips, while "difficult" uses more obstructive sounds and is a bit harder to say.
The word 'Mellifluous' actually sounds silky and smooth flowing, which happens to be it's exact dictionary definition.
